facts.fact: The kingdom is Hemkot; its capital is Taravan; the far valley is Neshar; the pass is the Shilak Pass; the last village below it is Kothi Shilak.
Heroine of Book 1 is Meera, 29, smuggler-guide and secret leader of the crew the wardens call the Salt Fox.
Hero of Book 1 is Rohan, 35, captain of the queen's pass-wardens on the Shilak side.
Kiran, 24 in Book 1, is Meera's younger brother and calls her Didi when afraid.
Ila, 30 in Book 1 and 31 in Book 2, is Rohan's younger sister and a crown pass-surveyor.
Kunal, 32 in Book 1 and 33 in Book 2, is prince of Neshar, nephew of Regent Pritam, and secret leader of the hill council rebels.

In winter the jogini let only rope-bound pairs cross a closed pass alive. Binding requires one hand-spun wool rope, the same knot tied on each other's wrist at a jogini cairn, and each speaking name and destination.
Ropes longer than twelve arm-spans are refused. Meera's red rope is eight arm-spans.

A bound pair cannot separate beyond the rope's length, tied or not, until meltwater first runs at the cairn where they were bound. Beyond the length both lose heat fast; at about twice the length the path vanishes and the mountain takes them.

Each lie to one's bound partner costs body heat in proportion to how much the truth would change the partner's choices. Small lie: white fingertips for an hour. Middling: frostnip and a night's shaking. Great: frostbite and dead flesh. A lie about the partner's life or death kills.
Silence, evasion, refusal, obvious jokes, lies to others and truths are free. Fire does not warm lie-cold.
A promise made while bound, if broken while still bound, strikes the breaker as a great lie.
Loophole: the partner lied to can take the lie-cold onto their own skin by touch; they then know a lie was told and its size, but not the truth, and they pay the cold themselves.
Bound pairs see the winter line marked by faint blue cairn-light at night. Armies cannot cross; only pairs bind, one pair per rope.
The Shilak Cairn's stones hum in wind and ring when a lie is told inside the ring.

The Closing Law, written 60 winters before Book 1, forbids crossing a high pass between first snow and first thaw on pain of hanging. Wardens cannot pardon; only the queen can. Sharing a fire with an unlawful crosser is harbouring, also a hanging crime.
A crown writ of passage signed by the queen's own hand makes a winter crossing lawful. Anyone named on it enters the Closing Roll and owes winter service for life.
The queen's seal is a lapis stone cut with a mountain goat. Rohan carries it in his coat; it must be pressed before the Neshar assembly at the Snow Fair to revoke Regent Pritam's claim.
Meera carries twelve packets of redbark powder for the grey cough in Ranu. The crates bore a crown stamp that had been scraped off.
Rohan carries the clean-cut end of Dilan's rope in his coat.
Meera keeps waxed ledgers she calls the count, recording every person and packet carried and every price.
Meera's red rope was spun from wool sold by Lata's house in Taravan.
Rohan has twenty days from the start of Book 1 to reach the Snow Fair.
Jassi, 40, Meera's goat handler and second, dies in the avalanche in Book 1 chapter 3. He stays dead.
In Book 1 chapter 26 Meera loses the ring and little fingers of her left hand to one great lie about Kiran. Permanent.
Kiran has a frostbitten ear from the crossing on which Dilan died, two winters before Book 1.
Dilan, 23, Rohan's youngest warden, died two winters before Book 1 after cutting his own rope to keep Kiran from being dragged off the ice.
Varun, 38, Rohan's lieutenant, is Regent Pritam's man. He chose the approach route, set off the avalanche and sells stolen crown redbark to Meera's crew through a middleman.
The Rope-Hut is a stone shelter below the Long Saddle on the far side, with one chulha, one sleeping shelf and a limited juniper woodpile.
The Long Saddle is the high snowfield of the Shilak Pass, two days across.
Ranu is the fever village in lower Neshar; its healer is Nimmi, 50.
Garh Neshar is the regent's seat with a brass assembly bell; the Snow Fair is held on the frozen river meadow below it.
Rohan has hanged two lowland smugglers in three winters and seized Meera's crew's loads twice. He secretly pays poor families' seizure fines from his wage.
Meera charges rich clients double so poor ones cross free.
Asha, 28 in Book 1, leads a rival smuggler crew from the lower salt road and is paid by Varun to track the seal in Book 1.
Tej, 43 in Book 1, is Regent Pritam's general. He refuses the order to fire Ranu in Book 1 chapter 27 and is exiled after the Snow Fair as the regent's man.

Lata, 40 in Book 1, widowed wool trader of Taravan. Her husband Mohit died of fever in Neshar four winters before Book 1. She and Tej loved each other young; his soldiers burned her family's wool sheds in the Neshar Rising, 20 winters before Book 1.
Queen Sarala, 61, rules Hemkot, ill but alive. Book 1 is the 30th winter of her reign.
Regent Pritam, 51, regent of Neshar and Kunal's uncle, plans to be invested as ruler at the Snow Fair on the claim that the queen is dying.
The Old Bargain: founders Saro (a warden) and Hemi (a smuggler) first crossed Shilak bound about 300 winters ago. The original price was a promise; the crown later recast it as a death.
The last Bargain payment, 60 winters before Book 1, was Rohan and Ila's grandfather, a warden who walked into the snow. The Closing Law was written the next spring.
The Shilak Cairn's inner face is carved with two hands bound by one rope. The Under-Cairn carving reads 'carried till no thaw'.
Asha ties every knot in her grandmother's pattern, which matches the cairn carving and is Hemi's knot.
At Book 1's thaw the jogini warn through the cold that the Old Bargain is unpaid and the pass will close forever after the fourth winter unless someone pays.
Book 1 ends with Meera and Rohan retying an ordinary rope by choice after the bond ends, as their betrothal, and drafting the Winter Crossing Law.
Rohan's form of address for Meera is Guide; hers for him is Captain, until it changes.
Kunal is the masked buyer who pays for Ranu's medicine in Neshar silver stamped with a cut corner.
The queen's seal wax is mixed with her own blood, proof she sealed it herself.
Roop and Chand are the last crew pair to cross back from Ranu, bound to each other until the thaw. Roop carries Kiran's note.
Jassi names his pack goats Pomegranate, Auntie, Sheriff, Magistrate and Judge.
Wardens make a sweep of Kothi Shilak every tenth day, so Meera expected a patrol on the day Rohan arrives.
The brass button left as the token for the next drop is small, domed, plain and brand new with a stiff shank. The next courier is to carry its twin, and without the twin no crate is released.
Kiran's note gives Nimmi's tally as forty-one sick, nine of them under ten, and six buried.

The Closing Law notice is nailed to the left gatepost of Kothi Shilak, and the hanging tree is a deodar just outside the gate with one peg hammered into the trunk per hanging. Two pegs are pale from last winter.
Meera, with Bindu's help, hides the redbark in the middle of one of Bindu's raw wool bales. They have rehearsed this for four winters.
Hakam is the three-fingered old man of Kothi Shilak whom Meera points out in the yard.
Rohan's party for the crossing is two wardens (Rohan and Varun) and two guides (Jassi and Meera); the other wardens return to the post.
Rohan has told Varun, and no one else beyond the queen, that he carries the queen's seal.
Wardens carry an iron probe spike used to find salt in grain; the salt house wool bales were probed to arm's depth with it but not cut open.
Varun's coat has one new brass button among pewter ones; he claims a pedlar sold it to him after he lost a button on the stair.
Widow Puja's seizure fine is eighteen silver, for salt found in her late husband's lean-to; Rohan pays it secretly.
Meera tells the yard her mother died of the grey cough ten winters ago because medicine was on the wrong side of the law.
The warden report of Dilan's death records blood on the ice and a curl of frozen cartilage no longer than a fingernail, which Rohan reads as the rim of an ear.
Rohan knows a warden who lets a known load cross is harbouring it by the letter of the Closing Law; he writes no report and decides to follow the redbark toward the Salt Fox.
The wool bales (Bindu's, with the hidden redbark) stand in the goat pen beneath the salt house; the wardens search the pen last.

Badami is Jassi's old bell-goat, too old for crossings, left in the salt-house pen. Jassi carries her kid-days bell on a thong at his collar; she is to retire with him to his sister's orchard of forty apricot trees.
Meera takes Badami's small dented brass kid-bell from Jassi's fist and keeps it buttoned in her coat with Kiran's note.
Rohan has two or three cracked ribs on his left side and cannot raise his left arm above the shoulder.
Of the five pack goats, Pomegranate and Auntie are dug out dead; the other three are never found. All the wardens' probes and tent poles are lost or left behind.
Rohan believes Varun was buried in the slide and is dead; Meera heard an iron ring before the first crack but has not interpreted it.
Meera gave Rohan odds: about one in four the gully slides, one in three the face cornice; Varun chose the gully as the lesser risk.
The twelve redbark packets are small palm-sized bundles of waxed paper tied with thread, laid in three rows of four inside the oilcloth roll at the bottom of Meera's pack.
Meera and Rohan bet on whether he can stay silent for an hour; the stake is the loser's sattu at the next halt, which Rohan wins and will collect then.
A waystone stands at the foot of the climb to the Long Saddle: a squat grey pillar with a shelf of flat stones left by earlier crossers. Meera builds a three-stone cairn there for Jassi.
Because Meera's fingertips are white from the demonstration lie for an hour, Rohan notes they cannot testify to anything she says during that hour.
The shelf at the waystone hides a cache of old dried dung cakes under the lowest slab, left by goat-crews for the next crossers; an unwritten mountain custom Meera knows.
Meera has carried two hundred and six people across the pass, not counting salt, and has written each in her ledger; she tells Rohan this number in the question trade.
The Shilak Cairn's two-hands-and-rope carving is also on the waystone's east face, worn smooth.
Meera and Kiran, as children, once played at the end of a rope and felt the rope's cold; their mother screamed.

The winter Meera was fifteen (fourteen winters before Book 1), on her first bound crossing with her mother, she went back for a dropped mitten a few paces past the rope's length and felt the rope's cold; her mother screamed. This replaces the earlier childhood-rope-play fact; Kiran is not part of the memory.

The waystone at the foot of the Long Saddle climb hums low in wind and rises in pitch, with its blue cairn-light thickening, when a lie is told to a bound partner nearby; it stays low and level at a true answer. This extends F015 beyond the Shilak Cairn.

The warden chronicle phrase, from the first chronicle of the Shilak post, reads: 'Two brothers in arms. They crossed the closed pass bound by one rope, and the pass has stood open to the faithful ever since.' Crews tell it as a warden and a smuggler.
Rohan hunted the Salt Fox crew for one winter because the law required it, and has hunted it two more winters for Dilan's sake; Meera notes the exact accounting.
Jassi's spare cord is a braided goat-hair line he used to tether kids; Meera carries it in her pack and uses it to bind Rohan's ribs.
Rohan's cracked ribs are the seventh and eighth on the left side; he also cannot raise the left arm above the shoulder (matches F068).
Rohan carries a grey warden-issue pattu, smelling of camphor, rolled at his belt; it survived the avalanche.

The ribs lie happens at first light on the pitch above the waystone; the pair shelter in a hollow under the Saddle's lip for the day and night, losing a day, and Meera shakes through the night. Nineteen of Rohan's twenty days remain.
Meera first calls Rohan by his given name here, unnoticed by her, while he calls her Meera at the end.

The ribs lie happens at first light on the pitch above the waystone, with seventeen of Rohan's twenty days remaining at that dawn. The pair shelter in a hollow under the Saddle's lip for the day and night, losing a day, so sixteen remain by the following night. Meera shakes through the night.

Rohan's writ is a folded creamy paper with red wax, carried in a boiled-leather writ case stamped with a goat. Meera cuts a strip from the case to make snow goggles, and Rohan moves the paper inside his coat.
Asha's crew is recognisable by packs covered in onion-skin ochre canvas.

The crew ledge is a shelf cut by Bindu's mother forty winters ago into the cornice on the south face, with iron pegs and a cache of three days' food and two dry blankets. It is reached across a gully with an eight-pace snow bridge.
Rohan tells Meera that he carries a thing the regent's side would pay a lordship for, and that he believes the four pursuers have been told where to find him. He declines to name it.
Meera infers from the two ropes that Asha's four are two bound pairs who each spoke their true names at the Shilak Cairn, and that someone paid them enough to do it.
Rohan wonders aloud who knew his route, saying it was chosen for him and only a handful saw it.
Meera tells a small lie to Rohan ('I don't care a fig for the shelf'); her right fingertips whiten for an hour and Rohan reads it from her hand.
The Rope-Hut has a sprig of juniper nailed above its door and a door facing downhill; it lies about an hour's descent by cairn-light from the crew ledge on the south slope.
Asha's four, after losing the tracks on the bare ridge, cast east along the Saddle's lip rather than finding the ledge.
Meera hauls Rohan out of the gully with a sliding-grip two-to-one drag on the red rope anchored to her axe, which Bindu calls the lazy woman's lift.
The crown redbark wrappers carry a faint round sieve-mark pressed into the wax along the fold, from the lowland guild stores' silk sieve with a ring in the weave.
The regent's hunters announce themselves with a two-note falling horn call that Meera recognises, and they climb the Neshar-side road with torches in a long line of fourteen or more.
Dilan's rope end is a forearm's length of grey hand-spun wool, rolled and tied with a scrap of its own cord. One end is whipped with black thread (Dilan's own neat work); the other is the clean cut.
Rohan swore at the Shilak warden hall, before eleven wardens, with Dilan's rope end in his hand, to find the one who stood at its far end.
Dilan was bad at knots except the black-thread whipping, could not carry a tune, and sang a hymn every watch that he mistook for a love song.

Meera's firewood rule: one question each per night; a refusal burns one extra stick over the night's five. The hut holds thirty-six sticks at dusk of the first full day, enough for seven nights plus one.
Meera and Rohan decide to wait in the Rope-Hut a day while the regent's hunters camp under the Saddle's lip; the winter line meets the Neshar road at the third bend, half a day down.

Varun read the crossing party aloud at the post gate the night before: three wardens and two guides. Rohan struck the third warden's name at dawn, so only two wardens went into the gully. Meera heard this, so 'three wardens and two goat-folk' could only have come from the written plan.
Lalit is Asha's tracker, a thin young man bound to her by rope and carrying a spyglass. Asha's second pair stays at the camp, unnamed.
Asha gives Meera the whole day and the next until the light goes; after that she comes down with four.
Firewood count: thirty-one sticks after the first night, thirty after Rohan's first refusal, twenty-nine after the second.

Rohan knows the Neshar-side road from walking it as a boy with his father and from mapping the post's end of it. He names a herdsmen's cut above the third bend, behind a stone fold, and a shrine on the way.
Rohan has a lung fever with a rattling cough that has been building unspoken; it comes to a crisis at the end of chapter 10.

Firewood count (replaces earlier F110): thirty-one sticks in the bundle at the start of chapter 10's day; Meera takes the night's five (twenty-six left), then burns one stick for each of Rohan's two refusals (twenty-five, then twenty-four).

Revised: Varun read the crossing party over from his written sheet in the post room the night before, with the guides present: three wardens and two guides. Rohan struck the third name at dawn. So 'three wardens and two goat-folk' could only have come from the plan or someone in that room.

Meera deliberately withholds from Rohan that Asha's information came from the plan, because it came from his own post, she cannot yet rule him out, and it is leverage for Kiran's name. She notes that silence is free.

The queen's seal is a lapis stone about a thumb-joint long, threaded on a cord through a hole in its shoulder, tied off in a warden's double hitch (two turns round the standing part, a tuck, a locking half-turn), and sewn into a hidden pocket in the seam at the nape of Rohan's coat.
Meera's own habitual knot, taught by Bindu when she was five, is a flat reef with a half hitch; she unpicks it and ties the warden's double hitch instead.
Meera burns four sticks to boil the juniper pot and uses the hut's juniper sprig from above the door for the steam; the bundle is not recounted on the page.
The mountain goat appears on Hemkot's coins; the seal's goat is cut finer and differently.

A wind-felled juniper lies about ten paces downslope of the Rope-Hut door, just past the rope's eight-span reach from the sill; Meera burns its wet deadfall by day and saves the dry stick bundle for nights.

Asha's crew leaves a bundle hung in the deadfall juniper: sattu, dried apricots, a twist of salt and a strip of smoked goat, tied in the three-nested-loop knot that matches the cairn carving. Meera sketches it in the count and does not eat or decide its purpose yet.
Rohan takes a second half-pinch of redbark at first light this chapter; his fever has broken but he cannot walk.

The second man Rohan hanged was Ketan, seventeen, carrying forty pounds of salt to his mother in a high village; the first was an unnamed lowland runner of about thirty-one who carried powder for the regent's men. Rohan paid the mother's fine for the lean-to afterwards.
The Shilak post's file on the guides records only the high price of a crossing, not the double rate for the rich or the free crossings for the poor. Rohan has read it eleven times.

Asha's crew leaves a bundle hung in the deadfall juniper: sattu, dried apricots, a twist of salt and a strip of smoked goat, tied in the three-nested-loop knot that matches the cairn carving. Meera sketches it in the count as 'Same as cairn'. She eats a strip of the goat at noon; Rohan does not. She has not decided its purpose.

The second man Rohan hanged was Ketan, seventeen, a lowland boy from the Taravan road carrying forty pounds of salt over the closed pass to his mother, who had married into Neshar and had a cough. The first was an unnamed lowland runner of about thirty-one who carried powder for the regent's men. Rohan afterwards paid the fine the post levied on Ketan's mother.

Rohan's fallback route (the herdsmen's cut from the third bend behind the stone fold, past the shrine, round the spur to the Saddle's lip) was drawn at the post table two nights before the crossing, by Rohan with a ruler on a single copy in Varun's neat hand; only the two of them saw it.
Meera's rope signals: three short pulls mean halt, one long pull means come.

At dusk of this chapter the bundle holds nineteen dry sticks; five are burned for the night and a sixth for Meera's refusal, leaving thirteen. Nine days remain to the Snow Fair and they agree to move within two days.

knowledge.knows: The winter line over Shilak, the rope-craft and the lie-cold rule.
Rohan has hunted her crew for three winters.
Kiran froze an ear on a bad crossing two winters ago, but not that he was on Dilan's rope (learns Book 1 ch 22).
Her redbark comes through a lowland middleman; she does not know it is Varun (learns Book 1 ch 16).
The Closing Law, the regent's coup plan and the Snow Fair deadline.
His writ orders him to deliver the Salt Fox at the thaw; he does not know the Salt Fox is Meera (learns Book 1 ch 16).
A Kothi smuggler was on Dilan's rope; he does not know it was Kiran (learns Book 1 ch 29).
Varun chose the approach route; he does not suspect Varun until Book 1 ch 16.
His grandfather 'died on the pass' and believes it was an accident.
He was on Dilan's rope and Dilan cut it himself to save him; he kept Dilan's warden badge.
Varun pays her; the seal exists; her grandmother's knot pattern but not its meaning.
Her grandfather died on the pass 60 winters ago, not how.
His uncle's coup plan, three hidden summer routes, and that someone in the wardens sells crown medicine.
Tej's soldiers burned her family's sheds; Mohit died of fever in a closed winter. She does not know Tej spared Ranu (learns Book 3 midpoint).
He burned Lata's sheds under orders and still loves her.
The true story of the Old Bargain and that Rohan and Ila's grandfather was its last payer.
His own scheme; he does not know Meera is the Salt Fox.
His coup plan and Varun's sabotage of the approach.
Ranu's fever death count for three winters; later witnesses Tej lower the torches.

timeline.event: Saro and Hemi make the first bound crossing of Shilak and the Old Bargain; Hemi later dies of a great lie told to save Saro.
Rohan and Ila's grandfather walks into the snow as the Bargain's payment; the Closing Law is written the next spring.
The Neshar Rising; Tej's soldiers burn Lata's family wool sheds; Lata marries Mohit within the year.
Meera and Kiran's mother dies of fever during a closed winter; Meera, 19, begins smuggling.
Mohit dies of fever in Neshar during a closed winter.
Rohan begins hunting the Salt Fox crew.
Dilan cuts his own rope to save Kiran and dies on the pass; Kiran's ear is frostbitten.
Rohan arrives at Kothi Shilak hunting the Salt Fox; Meera prepares to cross with redbark.
Varun's avalanche kills Jassi; Meera and Rohan are rope-bound at the Shilak Cairn.
Rope-Hut midpoint: Meera admits she is the Salt Fox; Varun's betrayal deduced; first kiss and Rohan's promise.
Meera's great lie about Kiran costs two fingers.
Tej orders the torches lowered at Ranu.
Snow Fair: the seal is pressed and Pritam's claim revoked; Meera enters her ledgers into the record; Pritam imprisoned; Varun arrested; Tej exiled.
The bond ends; Meera and Rohan retie a rope by choice; the jogini warn that the Old Bargain is owed.
Queen Sarala signs the Winter Crossing Law.
Ila and Kunal's crossing and the Shared Map; the Under-Cairn found; Pritam escapes.
Lata and Tej's crossing; Tej pardoned on Lata's surety; the Bargain's original price is revealed as a promise; Kiran leaves to pay.
Kiran and Asha pay the Old Bargain with a lifelong promise; Queen Sarala dies at the thaw; the pass stays open forever.
